newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Troops deploy in Albania, demo set for Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: Troops deploy in Albania, demo set for Tuesday.

text.p: Albanian troops deployed around the country on Monday after a weekend of violent protests as ruling right-wing Democrats called for a counter-demonstration against rival Socialists they accuse of stoking the tension.

Armed soldiers surrounded the central bank and guarded state television headquarters in Tirana after a day of clashes in the capital, a prison riot and waves of demonstrations mainly in the south of the Balkan state.
Seven army trucks full of soldiers were seen parked around the Defence Ministry on central Skanderbeg Square, where protesters battled with riot police on Sunday.
Radio Tirana said soldiers had begun clearing roads near weekend flashpoints where protesters had erected barricades of rocks to prevent police reinforcements reaching their towns.

Troops had cleared one road near the town of Memaliaj, 190 km (120 miles) south of Tirana but the radio said units were still attempting to unblock the main route between Rrogozhine and Lushnje, where protesters hurled rocks at police on Saturday and physically attacked Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu.
Soldiers were acting under orders of President Sali Berisha, who assumed special powers on Sunday to try to take control of the biggest crisis of his five-year rule and head off further protests.
In an atmosphere of growing anarchy, two inmates were killed in a riot and failed breakout at a prison in central Albania late on Sunday.

"After they (the inmates) heard the main news, they tried to exploit the situation and wanted to break out of prison," said the deputy director-general of prisons, Bedri Coku. "They were influenced by the recent events of vandalism and destruction all over the country."
Coku said security had been stepped up at jails around the country but prison authorities would not hesitate to call in the army if trouble got out of control.

Radio Tirana reported one disturbance on Monday in the town of Peshkopi deep in the northern mountains some 180 km (110 miles) from the capital. Protesters had attacked police with stones, the radio said, but gave few other details.
The wave of unrest has been sparked by growing anger over the collapse of pyramid investment schemes in which Albanians have poured billions of leks (millions of dollars) in cash.
Thousands turned to violence when two of nine national schemes closed down, leaving some families destitute and others fearing their investments in other funds could also disappear.

Opposition parties, which boycotted a general election last May after accusing the Democrats of rigging the vote, have demanded Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi's government resign over its handling of the pyramid schemes and new polls.
The Democrats went on the offensive on Monday, calling for a peaceful counter-demonstration on Tuesday outside Socialist Party headquarters just off central Skanderbeg Square.
Foreign Minister Shehu, who is also Democratic Party chairman, told hundreds of supporters at an emotion-charged meeting in Tirana that left-wingers were to blame for provoking two weeks of protests.
"I invite you to gather tomorrow in front of Socialist Party headquarters...to protest peacefully against the leaders of this party," Shehu told some 700 chanting supporters.
Democratic Party backers shouted "We love the president" and "Down with communism, down with the red bastards".

Such a gathering was only likely to inflame an already tense atmosphere but the Democrats are intent on flexing their muscles after seeing many of their party offices torched in weekend demonstrations in the south.
In an attempt to appease desperate investors, the prime minister has pledged to pay Albanians all the money they have put into failed schemes with interest by February 5.
Authorities have frozen some $300 million placed in state banks by pyramid scheme operators but the sum was unlikely to be enough to compensate the thousands of Albanians fearing complete ruin.
